title: Java Strings and Immutability: Quick Revision
summary: Night-before notes on Java string immutability, the string pool, equals vs ==, StringBuilder, text blocks, immutable class design, records and defensive copies.

chapters.title: Immutability and the String Pool: The Mental Model
points: Immutable means state cannot change after construction; every String method (concat, replace, toUpperCase, trim) returns a NEW String and leaves the original untouched

String is final and its value is private, so no subclass or caller can mutate it; that is what makes it thread-safe, safely cacheable as a HashMap key (hash computed once) and usable for security-sensitive values like paths
String pool: a JVM-wide table of unique string literals on the heap; a literal reuses the existing pooled object, so "a" == "a" is true
new String("a") always creates a separate heap object outside the pool; s.intern() returns the pooled instance, so new String("a").intern() == "a" is true
Compile-time constants are folded and pooled ("a" + "b" == "ab" is true); a concatenation involving a non-final variable happens at runtime and creates a new object (false)

chapters.title: equals vs == and Comparing Strings
points: == compares references (same object?); equals() compares content; for Strings you almost always want equals()
String s1 = "hi"; String s2 = "hi"; String s3 = new String("hi"); then s1 == s2 is true, s1 == s3 is false, s1.equals(s3) is true
Put the literal first to avoid NullPointerException: "admin".equals(input), or use Objects.equals(a, b) when both may be null
equalsIgnoreCase for case-insensitive content match; compareTo returns negative, zero or positive for ordering (lexicographic by char value) and is used for sorting
Overriding equals requires overriding hashCode too: equal objects must have equal hash codes, or HashMap and HashSet lookups silently fail

chapters.title: StringBuilder and Efficient String Building
points: StringBuilder is a mutable char sequence with an internal resizable buffer; append, insert, delete, reverse and setCharAt modify it in place and return this, enabling chaining
Concatenating with += in a loop creates a new String every iteration (O(n^2) copying); use one StringBuilder and call toString() at the end
StringBuilder vs StringBuffer vs String: String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and not thread-safe (fast, default choice); StringBuffer is mutable and synchronized (rarely needed)
Example: new StringBuilder().append("a").append(1).reverse().toString() gives "1a"; pre-size with new StringBuilder(capacity) when the length is known to avoid regrowth
A single-expression concatenation (a + b + c) is already optimized by the compiler, so a builder only pays off inside loops; String.join and Collectors.joining are cleaner for delimited lists

chapters.title: Text Blocks
points: A text block is a multi-line string literal delimited by triple quotes ("""), with the content starting on the line after the opening delimiter (Java 15+)

Incidental indentation is stripped: the compiler removes the common leading whitespace, using the closing delimiter's position as part of that calculation; move the closing """ left to keep more indent
Newlines are kept as \n; end a line with a backslash to suppress the line break, and use \s to preserve a trailing space (trailing spaces are otherwise stripped)
Quotes and double quotes need no escaping inside, which suits JSON, SQL and HTML: String json = """\n {"id": 1}\n """;
A text block is still an ordinary String, interned like any literal; use formatted(args) or String.format for placeholders, since there is no interpolation

chapters.title: Immutable Classes, Records and Defensive Copies
points: Recipe for an immutable class: declare it final, make all fields private final, set them only in the constructor, provide no setters, and never return mutable internals
final on a field makes the reference unassignable, not the object immutable: a final List or Date field can still be mutated through its methods

Defensive copy in and out: copy mutable arguments in the constructor (new ArrayList<>(list), date.clone()) and return copies or unmodifiable views from getters (List.copyOf, Collections.unmodifiableList); otherwise callers can change your state

record Point(int x, int y) {} generates a private final field per component, a canonical constructor, accessors x() and y(), equals, hashCode and toString; it is implicitly final and cannot extend a class
Records are shallowly immutable: a List component is still mutable, so use a compact constructor to validate and copy: record Team(List<String> names) { Team { names = List.copyOf(names); } }

chapters.title: Strings and Immutability Cheat Sheet
points: Strings: immutable, final, pooled literals; methods return new Strings, so always assign the result (s = s.trim())
Compare: equals for content, == for reference only; "lit".equals(x) or Objects.equals is null-safe; intern() returns the pooled copy
Build: StringBuilder in loops (single-threaded), StringBuffer only if shared across threads, String.join for delimited lists
Text blocks: """ on its own opening line, closing-delimiter position sets indent, \ joins lines, \s keeps trailing space, formatted() for values
Immutable design: final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies in and out, List.copyOf; records are shallowly immutable, so copy mutable components in the compact constructor
